title: The Thousand Martyrs Cup: Football Returns to Palestine After Three Years of Genocide
author: Abubaker Abed

training session ahead of the Thousand Martyrs Cup. August 2026. Courtesy of
Ittihad Deir al-Balah.

On a dirt field in the dense coastal neighborhood of Deir al-Balah last week,
players from Ittihad Deir al-Balah--one of Gaza's three standing football
clubs--gathered their torn balls, scuffed training cones, and rusted
equipment. Surrounded by rubble and with Israeli drones buzzing overhead, they
were preparing to train for a football tournament, the first in Palestine
since 2023.

Last month, the Palestinian Football Association (PFA) announced the return of
football to clubs across Palestine and Lebanon after a three-year hiatus
marked by Israel's genocide in Gaza, terrorism in the occupied West Bank, and
a brutal war on Lebanon. The resumption of the football association's leagues
in Gaza, the West Bank, Jerusalem, and Palestinian refugee camps in Lebanon
will open on September 4 with the Thousand Martyrs Cup, a two-month tournament
named for the more than 1,000 Palestinian athletes killed by Israel since
October 7, 2023.

Over 240 clubs are participating in the tournament: 50 clubs in Gaza, 165 in
the West Bank and Jerusalem, and 28 clubs in Lebanon. Opening games will
simultaneously kick off at 6 p.m. Jerusalem Time on Friday. Matches in Gaza
will be played on four chewed-up artificial turf five-a-side football courts,
including Ittihad Deir al-Balah's playground. In the West Bank, Jerusalem, and
Lebanon, the matches will be played on standard eleven-a-side pitches.

Players and coaches told Drop Site News they have mixed feelings about the
resumption of Palestinian football, with Israel's violence making life all but
impossible, while at the same time wanting to pay tribute to the martyrs and
stand resilient.

Yet it is unclear if players in Gaza will be able to even show up to the
tournament, the assistant coach of Ittihad Deir al-Balah, Motaz Rabia, told
Drop Site News. He said the continued daily Israeli airstrikes and relentless
attacks have forced the team's training sessions to be cancelled and have
restricted players' movement.

Just last week, Israeli fighter jets bombed the neighbourhood adjacent to the
club building in Deir al-Balah as well as the Abu-Salim Mosque downtown. On
Saturday, an Israeli airstrike on a motorcycle in the Jabaliya refugee camp in
northern Gaza killed Khadamat Jabaliya club star Abdel-Fattah Abu-Aish, less
than a week before the tournament.

Every club in Gaza has suffered tremendous losses. Ittihad Deir al-Balah alone
lost at least ten players, staffers, and coaches in Israeli attacks, including
Asian Football Confederation-approved manager Hani Al-Mosadar and star
midfielder Nasrallah Al-Mqataa. Other players have been forced to quit
football to try and provide bare life essentials for their families.

At least 1,013 athletes have been killed by Israel in Gaza and the West Bank
since October 2023, according to the PFA, including nearly 570 footballers,
over 100 of them children. The Israeli military has also destroyed or damaged
nearly 270 sports facilities in Gaza, including nine out of 10 stadiums and 51
out of 54 club facilities.

The PFA spokesperson in Gaza, Mustafa Siyam, told Drop Site he hopes the
tournament will restore "some semblance of normalcy" for Gaza's footballers
and mark the "start of a new chapter" for football in the devastated enclave.

In Gaza, a historically intense derby between Khadamat Rafah and Shabab Rafah
will kick off the Thousand Martyrs Tournament: Two rivals from a once-vibrant
city, now razed and occupied by Israeli forces. Meanwhile, Jabal Al-Mokaber
will play against Shabab Al-Khalil in the opening match in the West Bank. Al-
Ansar will take on Al-Nahda in Lebanon.

"Despite Israel's deliberate targeting of athletes and ban on the entry of
football equipment, we are very keen on reviving football activities for our
players," Siyam said. "This tournament carries many messages, especially since
it bears the names of our very dear players who were killed during the
genocide. It also holds out hope for a better future for football in Gaza."

## **" Israel blocks footballs"**

The Ittihad Deir al-Balah football club has barely been able to hold training
sessions once or twice a week ahead of the tournament, and scarcely has any
equipment to function with daily Israeli airstrikes and an ongoing crippling
siege, according to Rabia.

"We can't afford a training ball. Israel blocks footballs. One flat ball now
costs around $400. Our players can't afford the food to rebuild their fitness
and physicality. We're very reluctant to participate, but we're playing to
honor our martyred players and staffers," Rabia told Drop Site. "We have
players now displaced in the southernmost part of Gaza. We can't even cover
their transportation fees and bring them to play. Therefore, we have called up
the youths."

Rabia said that football means a lot to everyone at the club and that their
continued involvement is emblematic of their steadfastness.

"Sports unite people. In Gaza, football has died. We have so much talent and
potential for the world, but we are completely shrugged off. I hope FIFA
listens to us and treats us as human beings. We deserve to be seen and take
our chances," he lamented.

"All we want to see in Gaza now is an actual ceasefire because it doesn't
exist," he added. "I wish to wake up one day without more bombings and
casualties. And we hope to see justice in this world where basic human rights
and rules apply to all, including Palestinians."

Under its president Gianni Infantino, FIFA controversially took part in
President Donald Trump's so-called Board of Peace, which has been tasked with
overseeing Gaza, and pledged to reconstruct Gaza's football infrastructure
through a $75 million plan announced at the inaugural meeting in February.
There has been zero progress on the plan so far.

Siyam, the PFA spokesperson, told Drop Site that the association was not
informed of the details of the alleged FIFA plan but said any support was
"welcome" and urged FIFA to expedite it.

Meanwhile, Israel has routinely violated the "ceasefire" that went into effect
in October 2025, killing over 1,300 Palestinians and wounding over 4,400,
according to Gaza's Health Ministry, while severely restricting the entry of
life essentials, humanitarian aid, medical supplies, and reconstruction
materials and equipment. The Israeli military has also continued to encroach
on Palestinian land, pushing the "yellow line" that demarcates its line of
control further westward where it now occupies nearly 70% of the Gaza Strip.

## **" I may be killed in the next 15 minutes"**

Mohammed Al-Taramasi, 26, who plays right back for Shabab Jabaliya Club and
Palestine's Olympic Team, lives in a dilapidated tent in the Jabaliya refugee
camp close to the "yellow line" where he is forced to survive daily artillery
shelling, shooting, and attacks from tanks and quadcopters from Israeli troops
nearby.

Al-Taramasi was displaced from his home nearly three years ago when Israeli
warplanes carpet bombed his neighborhood in the camp on October 28, 2023,
killing his father and dozens of extended family members. He somehow survived
the attack and buried his father, whom he described as "his backbone".

"I used to wake up for my training. Now, gunshots terrify my family and me in
the morning," Al-Taramasi told Drop Site. "I am now talking to you on the
phone and I may be killed in the next 15 minutes. My father was killed. I am
displaced. I missed out on offers from Egypt and Libya in 2024 because I
couldn't leave Gaza. My life resembles hell on earth," he said, choking up
with grief and sorrow.

"There are two sides of the tournament: positive and negative," he continued.
"Positive because it is a tribute to our colleagues on the football stage.
Negative because we're not getting paid enough and the cup may have to be
called off. It's a nerve-wracking situation for all of us. But I wish to lift
the trophy for the sake of the slain footballers and my teammates and
neighbors."

Al-Taramasi said he hopes international football bodies and media outlets
would focus more on the plight of Gaza's football players and that many of
them have the potential to embark on stellar careers if only they were given
the same attention as players abroad.

from Ittihad Deir al-Balah football club train on a dirt playground ahead of

Outside of Palestine, Palestinian footballers living in exile also face
enormous challenges. Palestinian playmaker and winger Mohammed Hamada, 25,
plays for Al-Okhwa Club in the Saida refugee camp in Lebanon. Hamada's
grandparents were forced from their home in Acre, on the northern coastline of
historic Palestine, during the Nakba in 1948. Palestinian refugees in Lebanon
are unable to return to or visit any part of Palestine, since Lebanon-approved
travel documents are not recognized by Israeli authorities and they cannot
apply for a visa to enter the Occupied Territories.

Similar to Palestinian athletes in Gaza and the West Bank who are denied
permits by Israel to travel, Mohammed has had opportunities to play abroad,
but his precarious status in Lebanon with no passport and only a travel
document left him unable to pursue his dreams. Ahead of the tournament on
Friday, he says this cup means more than anything to him and he is eager to
play in honor of his people in Gaza.

"I can't enter Palestine. I have been heartbroken by what has been happening
during the last three years. Playing in this tournament is so emotionally
overwhelming that I can't put it into words," he said in a quavering voice. "I
am determined to win the trophy to pay the finest tribute to the thousand
martyrs. This tournament will offer us a chance to convey our message as
football players, and football is a great avenue for speaking up."

"I hope the world looks more at Gaza and Palestine," he added. "It's enough of
what has already transpired. I want all the international support,
particularly from FIFA and football associations, to go to the players in Gaza
and Palestine. We all failed Gaza, no matter what we do."
